solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Contaminated waters getting into brew, charge supplier?

indicators.note: getting into says one set of letters is placed inside the other word

parts.note: a brew is a potion

indicators.note: contaminated water is spoilt and altered, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Polluted water seeping into someone's drink, and a question about who supplies the bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' looks like a fee, but it is electrical charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A power station generates electricity, supplying electrical charge to the grid, hence the playful question mark.

clue.text: Tool was in the van, smashed

parts.note: a pick is a digging tool
being in the van, the vanguard, means you led

explanation.surface: A tool in a van that gets broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'van' is short for vanguard, the front, not a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Pickled and smashed are both slang for very drunk.

clue.text: Giant scream heard?

indicators.note: heard says the word for scream is spoken, giving a word that sounds the same

parts.note: a wail is a long scream or cry

explanation.surface: Was that an enormous scream someone heard?
explanation.definitionFit: A whale is a giant, used for anything enormous, as in a whale of a time.

clue.text: Delegate in the canteen explaining once more

parts.note: a rep, a representative, is a delegate
in a canteen you would be eating

explanation.surface: A union delegate in the works canteen, going over the point again.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeating means saying something again, so explaining once more is going over it a second time.

clue.text: Ace removed from pack of cards, red

indicators.note: removed from says a letter is taken out of the word that follows

parts.note: tarot is a pack of cards used in fortune telling
A is the abbreviation for ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: The ace pulled from a deck, which shows a red card.
explanation.walkthrough: 'red' looks like a card colour but means a left-winger.
explanation.definitionFit: A Trot is a Trotskyist, and red is slang for any communist or left-wing radical.

clue.text: Dessert rising after nuts taken out of it

indicators.note: after says the reversed dessert comes behind the scrambled letters
nuts means crazy, so these letters are scrambled
rising in a down clue says the word reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: pud is short for pudding, a dessert

explanation.surface: A pudding whose nuts have been removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of it' looks like part of the nut removal, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being out of it is slang for drunk, as is being tanked up on alcohol.

clue.text: Better, having dismissed gathering

parts.note: a batsman dismissed in cricket is out
a do is a party or social gathering

explanation.surface: An improvement, now the meeting has been sent away.
explanation.definitionFit: To better someone is to surpass them, to beat their performance.

clue.text: Is nothing in NI city ridiculous?

indicators.note: in says the first pieces go inside the city name

parts.note: Derry, or Londonderry, is a city in Northern Ireland (NI)
O is the round figure for nothing, zero

explanation.surface: A question whether a Northern Irish city has nothing worth mocking.
explanation.definitionFit: Derisory means laughably small or inadequate, so absurd or ridiculous.

clue.text: Cross somewhat resized on keyboard

indicators.note: somewhat says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Someone a bit annoyed at a keyboard that got resized.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry, but it is a hybrid animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A zedonk is a hybrid, the offspring of a zebra and a donkey.

clue.text: Limiting measure, a hundred light feathers

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a lamp is a light
down is soft fine feathers

explanation.surface: A curious inventory: a restriction, a hundred lamps and some feathers.
explanation.definitionFit: A clampdown is a crackdown, a measure imposed to restrict or limit some activity.

clue.text: Central idea in the home, not house

indicators.note: not tells us to leave out the named letters from the phrase beside it

explanation.surface: The central idea of a household rather than of the building itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes HO from THE HOME, leaving the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A theme is the main subject or underlying idea running through a work.

clue.text: Insignificant returns in amateur play

indicators.note: in places the turned word inside the word for amateur

parts.note: lay means non-professional, as in a lay person

indicators.note: returns says the word for insignificant is read backwards

parts.note: wee means tiny, insignificant

explanation.surface: A trivial contribution made in an amateur dramatic production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'play' is not drama here but slack, as in play in a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Play means room to move or freedom of action, the same as slack or latitude.

clue.text: Cry when jumping child falls back into earth

indicators.note: into places the reversed word inside the word for earth

parts.note: geo- is the combining form meaning earth, as in geology

indicators.note: falls back says the word for child is reversed

parts.note: a minor is a child in law

explanation.surface: A cry as a child tumbles backwards into the soil while jumping about.
explanation.walkthrough: GEO for earth comes from the Greek prefix seen in geology.
explanation.definitionFit: Paratroopers and others shout this exclamation as they leap, a traditional cry before a jump.

clue.text: Fail to lasso equine, African mammal

indicators.note: to lasso is to rope around something, so one word goes around the other

parts.note: to die is to fail, as an engine dies
an ass is an equine animal

explanation.surface: A cowboy failing to rope a horse-like animal somewhere in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: The dassie is the rock hyrax, a small furry mammal of southern Africa.

clue.text: Vessel that sails?

parts.note: a drinking vessel for sherry or beer shares its name with a sailing ship with fore-and-aft rigging

explanation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' reads as a boat, but the clue nods to a glass too.
explanation.definitionFit: A schooner is both a tall glass for drinks and a fore-and-aft rigged sailing ship.

clue.text: Cream buns worryingly close!

indicators.note: worryingly suggests the letters are disturbed and rearranged

parts.note: to lock is to close, as a door

explanation.surface: Cream buns sitting alarmingly near, a temptation for a dieter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worryingly' rearranges BUNS into SUNB. 'Cream' looks like part of a cake order but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sunblock is a lotion, a protective cream applied to the skin against sunburn.

clue.text: Necessary to admit playful line is stupid

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the money word takes the rearranged letters inside

parts.note: the necessary is slang for money, as is brass

indicators.note: playful says the letters are toyed with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A dim person must be allowed a jokey remark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playful' scrambles LINE into AINLE. 'The necessary' and 'brass' are both British slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Brainless describes someone foolish or witless, lacking any intelligence.

clue.text: Uncivil on the Isle of Wight ferry?

definitions.text: on the Isle of Wight ferry?
definitions.meaning: read as two words, the ferry crossing to the Isle of Wight takes you into the Solent, the strait between it and the English mainland

explanation.surface: A rude passenger on the boat to the Isle of Wight.
explanation.definitionFit: Insolent means rude and disrespectful, the opposite of civil and polite.

clue.text: Wood finding tree, old golfer stymied?

indicators.note: stymied, a golfing term for being blocked, says one word is trapped inside another

parts.note: may is the hawthorn tree
Ben Hogan was a famous American golfer of the mid twentieth century

explanation.surface: A veteran golfer blocked by a tree on the course, and a wood club involved.
explanation.walkthrough: Stymie is an old golf term for a ball blocking the line to the hole; 'Wood' also suggests a golf club.
explanation.definitionFit: Mahogany is a reddish-brown hardwood timber prized for furniture.

clue.text: No way I'm hopping on that!

definitions.meaning: an exclamation of flat disbelief or refusal
someone hopping is standing on a single foot of their own

explanation.surface: A refusal to jump on board with a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: My foot! is an idiom of scornful disbelief, the same as saying no way.

clue.text: Preserve that deep valley

parts.note: to can food is to preserve it
yon is an old or dialect word for that, as in yon hill

explanation.surface: An instruction to protect a particular gorge.
explanation.definitionFit: A canyon is a deep gorge cut by a river, a steep-sided valley.

clue.text: Two presents gone

definitions.meaning: two kinds of present side by side: the present moment and the present place, read together as one phrase
vanished, not to be found anywhere

explanation.walkthrough: 'presents' looks like gifts, but means present in time joined to present in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gone has vanished and cannot be found in any place at all.

clue.text: March to so distressingly penetrating beat

indicators.note: penetrating says the rearranged letters go inside the word for beat

parts.note: to flog is to beat

indicators.note: distressingly says these letters are upset and rearranged

explanation.surface: A soldier's grim march with a heavy drumbeat.
explanation.definitionFit: To footslog is to trudge or march laboriously on foot, especially for a long way.

clue.text: Stop running market stand

definitions.meaning: of an engine, to cut out and cease working
a booth or table for selling goods at a market

explanation.surface: Shutting down a stall at a market.
explanation.definitionFit: An engine stalls when it suddenly stops, and a stall is also a trader's stand.

clue.text: Article on why failing, regardless

parts.note: a is the indefinite article

indicators.note: failing suggests the words break down and their letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A newspaper piece about why something went wrong, published anyway.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyhow means in any case, carrying on whatever happens, the same as regardless.

clue.text: Island in heart of this nation

indicators.note: in places the island word inside those middle letters
heart of says take the middle letters of the word that follows

parts.note: an ait is a small island in a river

explanation.surface: An island at the centre of this country.
explanation.walkthrough: AIT (also eyot) is a small river island, especially in the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Haiti is a Caribbean country, an independent nation on the island of Hispaniola.

clue.text: English Prime Minister's blunted weapon

indicators.note: blunted says the end is taken off, as a blade's tip is dulled

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a British Prime Minister; the possessive just links him to the cut

explanation.surface: A British premier's sword with its edge dulled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blunted' drops the last letter of PEEL. Fencing foils and epees have blunted tips.
explanation.definitionFit: An epee is a thrusting sword used in fencing.

clue.text: A little co-operation works

indicators.note: a little says only a short run of letters is taken from inside the word that follows

explanation.surface: The modest claim that a bit of teamwork gets results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'works' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: musical works.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin opus means a work, and its plural is the word for several works.

clue.text: Old cat or dog I have, catching fifty rats, say?

parts.note: ex means former, old

indicators.note: catching says the pet word grabs a letter inside it

parts.note: a cat or dog is a typical pet
L is the Roman numeral for fifty
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A pet owner whose old cat or dog has caught fifty rats.
explanation.definitionFit: Rats! is a mild oath, an example of a swear word or exclamation of annoyance.

clue.text: Butterfly initially beats bird? One's talking nonsense!

indicators.note: initially says take the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: to lather someone is to beat or thrash them
a kite is a bird of prey

explanation.surface: A butterfly first outmatching a bird, scoffed at as nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: A blatherskite is a Scots term for a person who babbles foolishly, an incessant chatterer of rubbish.
